item.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study
item.description:
Background: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial.

Methods: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality.

Results: A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes.

Conclusions: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP.

item.title: Acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy: a critical synthesis of metabolic derangements and nutritional implications
item.description:
Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects up to 50% of critically ill patients and is frequently complicated by severe metabolic derangements, requiring the initiation of replacement therapy (RRT) in 10-15% of cases. Despite substantial progress in the diagnosis of AKI and optimisation of RRT delivery, the nutritional management of these patients remains an underexplored area.

Main body: AKI is increasingly recognised as a systemic metabolic disorder extending beyond impaired renal clearance. Key metabolic alterations include mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated gluconeogenesis, increased proteolysis and altered amino acid metabolism, with accelerated nitrogen wasting. These abnormalities are further amplified by acute systemic stress states, including sepsis, systemic inflammation, trauma, burns, liver dysfunction and multiorgan failure. RRT introduces additional metabolic consequences through extracorporeal losses of amino acids and micronutrients. Conversely, citrate anticoagulation, glucose-containing dialysate, and lactate-buffered solutions represent sources of clinically relevant calories. Current nutritional recommendations are largely extrapolated from heterogeneous intensive care populations. Available evidence suggests that AKI primarily influences energy balance rather than energy expenditure, which appears broadly comparable to that of other critically ill populations. While evidence specific to AKI is limited, protein provision of approximately 1.2-1.3 g/kg/day is generally recommended during critical illness. However, higher intakes of up to 1.7-2.5 g/kg/day may be considered in patients receiving RRT to offset extracorporeal amino acid losses and increased protein catabolism. In this setting, emerging concepts such as metabolic tolerance and biomarker-guided metabolic phenotyping may facilitate individualised nutritional strategies.

Conclusions: AKI, particularly when requiring RRT, is associated with profound and dynamic metabolic disturbances that substantially influence energy and protein requirements, thereby making nutrition an integral component of organ support therapies. Future research should evaluate precision nutrition strategies that tailor nutritional support to the phase of critical illness, measured energy expenditure, metabolic tolerance, and RRT-related nutrient losses and gains. Such studies should prioritise patient-centred outcomes, including physical function and recovery, in addition to nutritional and metabolic endpoints.

item.title: Prognostic relevance of protein prescriptions based on adjusted body weight in critically ill overweight or obese patients - analysis of a large international database
item.description:
Background: ESPEN currently recommends using adjusted body weight (aBW) to guide protein prescriptions for critically ill overweight or obese patients. The prognostic relevance of this concept is unknown.

Methods: We analyzed a subset of a large international point prevalence survey of nutritional practice in 785 intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Patients were included if they had been in the ICU for at least 96 h and had a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m². We modelled the association between early average protein intake (days 1-4 after ICU admission) and the cause-specific adjusted hazards of in-ICU death and ICU discharge alive within a competing risks framework. Intake was normalized to aBW, defined as ideal body weight plus 25% of the difference between actual and ideal body weight.

Results: 9,068 patients were analyzed. There was no evidence of an association between early protein intake and ICU discharge alive. In contrast, very low protein intake (below approximately 0.45 g/kg aBW/day) was associated with a higher hazard of in-ICU death. Above this threshold, there was no clear evidence of a further association between protein intake and the hazard of in-ICU death. The strongest association was observed at 0 g/kg aBW/day (adjusted hazard rate 1.41 i.e. an estimated 38% higher risk, 95% confidence interval 1.17-1.69).

Conclusions: Early protein intake does not appear to be associated with time to ICU discharge among survivors. However, in critically ill patients with overweight or obesity, very low protein intake during the early acute phase may be associated with less favorable in-ICU outcomes.

item.title: Conflict in intensive care units: a conceptual framework for patient, family, team, and inter-service disagreement
item.description:
For clinicians, conflict in the intensive care unit (ICU) is both common and expected owing to the nature of critical illness and its treatment. Examination of conflict in this context has been conceptually diffuse. Studies of moral distress, psychological safety, ethical climate, and other fields offer valuable insights that can be challenging to synthesize cohesively, due to differences in concepts, methods, and disciplinary perspectives. This narrative review integrates this literature using a task-process-relationship framework from organizational psychology. Conflict in the ICU arises in two principal arenas: between clinical teams and patients, families, or surrogates, and within and across clinical teams. Patients who retain decision-making capacity are a distinct and often overlooked party to conflict, as the focus has primarily been on the families and surrogates who speak for those who cannot. The task-process-relationship framework suggests a recurring escalation pattern for both arenas. Genuine task disagreements about treatment, prognosis, or goals of care can become destructive in the presence of process gaps or failures. These include role ambiguity, inconsistent messaging, and perceived unfairness. From there, conflict can enter the relationship domain wherein mistrust or identity threat makes resolution far harder, and two implications follow. First, much of what clinicians may describe as a "difficult family" can often be a response to antecedent process failures rather than a purely interpersonal problem, emphasizing the importance of engineering robust processes and systems in the ICU to avoid conflict reaching the relationship domain. Second, family and team conflict are linked in that unresolved team disagreement can reach families as contradictory recommendations and mixed messaging. Challenging family situations can expose team misalignment and damage collegial relationships. Evidence-based interventions, organized by conflict type and escalation stage, suggest that the most promising investments are structural, namely those built into rounds, improving role clarity, ensuring pre-conference team alignment, and fostering ethical climate. When conflict becomes entrenched, formal supports such as mediation and ethics consultation are matched to the nature of the dispute. While disagreement in intensive care is inevitable, destructive conflict is not.

item.title: Early albumin use and mortality in critically III children with severe hypoalbuminemia: a target trial emulation study
item.description:
Background: Hypoalbuminemia is highly prevalent in critically ill children and is an established independent risk factor for mortality. Whether albumin supplementation is associated with improved survival remains unclear, particularly in pediatric populations where causal evidence is sparse.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used data from the Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database, a single-center pediatric-specific critical care database in China, and adopted a target trial emulation (TTE) framework. Children whose first albumin measurement within 24 h of ICU admission was below 30 g/L were included (N = 1,649). Time zero was defined as the first detection of albumin below 30 g/L. The exposure was receipt of at least one dose of human albumin within 24 h after time zero. Primary outcomes were 7-day and 28-day all-cause mortality, estimated using IPTW-weighted Cox proportional hazards models with doubly robust adjustment. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding was assessed by E-value.

Results: Among 1,649 children, 374 (22.7%) received early albumin therapy. After doubly robust adjustment, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.24-0.74; P = 0.003; E-value = 4.21). The association with 28-day mortality was not significant (HR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.45-1.36; P = 0.393). Relaxing the hypoalbuminemia threshold to below 35 g/L attenuated the 7-day association (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.39-1.05). Extending the treatment window to 48 h further attenuated the association (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.40-1.91). A significant interaction was observed between vasoactive agent use and albumin therapy (P for interaction = 0.045), with the strongest association among children not receiving vasoactive agents (HR, 0.17; 95% CI, 0.04-0.70).

Conclusions: In critically ill children with severe hypoalbuminemia, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality. This association showed clear threshold- and time-dependence, suggesting that any potential benefit may concentrate within a narrow clinical window early in the disease course. Prospective confirmation is needed.

Trial registration: Not applicable. This is a retrospective observational study using de-identified data; the study protocol was not prospectively registered in a clinical trials registry.

item.title: Using capnography to differentiate airway from gastrointestinal placement of nasogastric tubes: a prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study
item.description:
Background: Patient safety incident reports and case reports have repeatedly highlighted factors contributing to inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes, including misleading pH readings, insufficiently documented placement checks, and misinterpretation of radiographs. The study aimed to: (i) evaluate the diagnostic performance of capnography compared with radiography for detecting inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes; and (ii) estimate the average cost incurred when radiography is used alone versus when capnography is used in conjunction with radiography.

Methods: A multicentre, prospective, observational diagnostic study was conducted. The diagnostic accuracy of capnography was examined using three end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds (> 5 mmHg, > 10 mmHg, > 15 mmHg), with radiographic confirmation as the reference standard. For each threshold, true positives, false negatives, true negatives, and false positives were determined. Cost savings per patient were estimated using a bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrapping method with 20,000 replications.

Results: A total of 508 participants were recruited from 39 study sites across 21 hospitals, including medical or geriatric wards, intensive care units, and emergency departments. Most participants (n = 485; 95.5%) had end-tidal carbon dioxide readings ≤ 5 mmHg. Radiography confirmed correct gastric placement in 452 cases (89.0%), with one case (0.2%) of inadvertent airway placement. Estimated cost savings per patient, were HK$210.3, HK$214.5, and HK$217.5 for the three respective end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds, based on a hypothetical strategy in which radiographic confirmation was performed only when the end-tidal carbon dioxide value exceeded a predefined threshold, compared with a radiography-only strategy in which all patients underwent radiographic confirmation of nasogastric tube placement.

Conclusions: Given the favourable outcomes and the simplicity of capnography measurement, capnography can be considered a first-line tool for excluding airway placement of nasogastric tubes, used alongside pH testing of aspirates.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, Number NCT05817864 (Registration date: 18 April 2023).

item.title: The evolution of biocontainment unit care for high-consequence infectious diseases: progress, lessons learned, and future directions
item.description:
Biocontainment units (BCUs) are specialized facilities designed to treat patients with high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) which are pathogens with high mortality rates, limited treatment options, and significant potential for healthcare-associated transmission. Since the opening of the first modern BCU in 1971, these units have evolved from simple isolation environments into advanced centers capable of delivering comprehensive critical care while maintaining rigorous infection control. This evolution has been driven from the lessons learned from past outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), among other emerging infectious threats. Four key domains contribute to the care of patients with HCIDs - laboratory capabilities, critical care delivery, healthcare workforce readiness, and safe patient transport. Improvements in diagnostic capabilities have allowed for earlier disease recognition while greater access to routine laboratory tests better inform clinical decision making. Clinical care capabilities now match those seen in intensive care units while maintaining infection control standards. Training of specialized workforce and multidisciplinary staffing models have improved bedside care and operational readiness. Meanwhile, innovations in ground and air transport have enhanced the ability to safely transfer HCID patients to facilities best suited to provide care. This review synthesizes the evolution of BCU capabilities globally, examining advances in critical care, diagnostics, investigational therapeutics, workforce models, and patient transport.

item.title: Sigh ventilation versus conventional protective ventilation in cardiac surgery: a proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Lung protective ventilation is crucial for preventing ventilator-induced lung injury in cardiac surgery. The protective role of a low tidal volume (VT) has been established, whereas the added protection afforded by lung recruitment remains uncertain. We investigated whether sigh breaths could provide additional lung protection, when added to protective ventilation with low VT.

Methods: This randomized, assessor-blinded, phase 2 proof-of-concept trial enrolled 192 patients undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery from February to August 2024. Patients were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive sigh ventilation (sigh breaths plus protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients) or conventional ventilation (protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients). Sigh breaths targeting a plateau pressure of 35 cmH2O (or 40 cmH2O for BMI >35 kg/m2) were delivered once every 6 min. Perioperative respiratory mechanics and gas exchange were monitored. The primary outcome was postoperative oxygenation, a marker of lung injury, as measured by the time-weighted average SpO2/FiO2 ratio during the first postextubation hour. There were 9 predefined secondary outcomes, including the severity of respiratory failure within postextubation day 7.

Results: All 192 patients completed the trial (53% male; median age, 64 [55-72] years). Perioperatively, sigh ventilation produced sustained improvements in oxygenation and respiratory system compliance, together with reductions in driving pressure and mechanical power (All P interaction<0.001). After extubation, the mean time-weighted SpO2/FiO2 ratio was higher in the sigh ventilation group (380 ± 86 vs 338 ± 93; mean difference 42.1, 95% CI [16.7 to 67.5]; P=0.001). The severity and occurrence of respiratory failure was reduced in the sigh ventilation group compared with conventional ventilation group (common odds ratio for lower severity 2.2; 95% CI [1.2 to 3.8]; P=0.007). There was no difference in adverse events of interest between groups.

Conclusions: In patients undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, adding sigh breaths was safe and resulted in a statistically significant improvement in postoperative oxygenation. Nevertheless, the clinical importance of this finding is uncertain because oxygenation was adequately maintained in both groups. Reduction in driving pressure and mechanical power, together with findings in secondary outcomes, suggest additional lung protection and justify future trials.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06248320); registered on January 30, 2024.

item.title: Dynamic reprogramming of alveolar epithelial-immune cell interactions in ARDS: from mechanisms to clinical translation
item.description:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by disruption of the alveolar-capillary barrier and refractory hypoxemia. Despite advances in supportive care, effective targeted therapies remain lacking. A major challenge to therapeutic success is the marked heterogeneity of ARDS, in which distinct biological mechanisms may drive different etiologies, inflammatory subphenotypes, and disease stages. Increasing evidence suggests that alveolar epithelial cells (AECs) are not merely passive targets of injury but active regulators of immune responses. Dynamic interactions between AECs and macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes occur throughout the course of ARDS and contribute to inflammatory amplification, tissue repair, and aberrant remodeling. In this review, we summarize epithelial-immune interaction patterns across the inflammatory exudative, proliferative repair, and fibrotic phases of ARDS. We further discuss how disease stage transitions, immunometabolic regulation, and ARDS heterogeneity shape these interaction networks. Based on these findings, we present an AEC-centered dynamic reprogramming framework that organizes current evidence on how epithelial-immune interactions change during ARDS progression. We also discuss candidate biomarkers, approaches for clinical stage and phenotype identification, therapeutic opportunities, and current evidence limitations, aiming to provide a conceptual framework for stage-specific and precision interventions in ARDS. We further contextualize existing and controversial immunomodulatory strategies, including corticosteroids and IL-6/IL-1 blockade, within this dynamic framework to illustrate how disease stage and patient phenotype may influence therapeutic responses. Throughout the review, we distinguish evidence derived from experimental models from observational data in human ARDS and separately identify human interventional evidence and therapies supported by current clinical guidelines.

item.title: Structural imbalances in open-access critical care research: a bibliometric analysis of abstracts from ICU database studies, 2018-2025
item.description:
Background: Open access intensive care unit (ICU) databases, including MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD), AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID-high time resolution ICU data set, and the Salzburg Intensive Care Database (SICdb), have fundamentally transformed critical care research over the past decade. Despite their widespread use, no comprehensive bibliometric analysis has systematically mapped the scientific output generated by studies relying on these resources.

Methods: A structured search was conducted in PubMed and Web of Science covering 2018 to 2025, retrieving original articles citing at least one of six defined open access ICU databases in title or abstract. Database selection followed the methodology of two prior systematic reviews of publicly available adult ICU datasets. Structured fields covering database used, machine learning (ML) methods, study design, clinical outcomes, AUROC values and patient counts were extracted via a semi-automated AI pipeline (DeepSeek API, multi-label JSON schema). The extraction pipeline was validated against a manually coded reference sample of 110 publications. Bibliometric analyses used R (bibliometrix v4.0.1) and Python. Citation counts, open-access status and SCImago journal quartile were retrieved via OpenAlex and SCImago to characterise the visibility and venue quality of the corpus. Four network analyses were performed: database-to-ML-method co-occurrence, country-to-database, international collaboration, and clinical topic co-occurrence networks.

Results: A total of 4,648 publications were included. Annual publication counts increased 45-fold from 42 (2018) to 1,907 (2025), accelerating markedly after 2021 following the release of MIMIC-IV. MIMIC-IV dominated database attributions (54.6%), followed by MIMIC-III (30.0%) and eICU-CRD (13.5%); European databases (AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID, SICdb) collectively accounted for only 1.9%. China contributed 65.6% of publications (n = 3,048) and the USA 10.6%. Median citations per paper were 5.0 (1.50 per year). 76.4% of publications were open access and 49.3% appeared in a Q1 SCImago-ranked journal. AUROC showed no meaningful correlation with citation impact (p = 0.10). Logistic regression was the most frequent ML method (38.5%), followed by neural networks (15.6%) and gradient boosting (13.8%). Retrospective observational designs dominated (67.9%), with mortality prediction in sepsis as the primary research focus. Median AUROC among 1,263 publications with extractable values was 0.798.

Conclusion: Open access database-based critical care research is growing almost exponentially, driven primarily by Chinese groups using MIMIC-IV for retrospective mortality studies. European databases remain underutilized. The field exhibits methodological homogeneity and a heavy bias toward US-American clinical practice patterns, with cross-dataset external validation rarely foregrounded in study abstracts. Greater use of European databases, systematic external validation and topical diversification are key priorities.

item.title: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial
item.description:
Background: Fluid resuscitation in early septic shock has a narrow therapeutic index. Signals of fluid intolerance are frequently present during early resuscitation, yet current resuscitation strategies do not incorporate them to guide when to limit fluid administration. We evaluated whether integrating fluid-intolerance signals as safety limits could reduce fluid-induced harm without compromising hypoperfusion resolution.

Methods: In this multicenter, open-label randomized trial in three Chilean ICUs, mechanically ventilated adults with septic shock, persistent hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness, and at least one high-risk criterion for fluid-induced harm were randomized 1:1 to a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy or standard care during a 6-hour protocol window. In the intervention arm, before each bolus, fluid-intolerance signals (lung ultrasound score, VExUS, E/lateral e', and central venous pressure) were graded as traffic-light: green received a 500-mL bolus, yellow 250 mL, and red no further fluid. Standard care delivered 500-mL boluses while hypoperfusion and fluid responsiveness persisted. The primary outcome was the change in PaO2:FiO2 from baseline to 6 h (ΔPaO2:FiO2).

Results: Recruitment was discontinued before the planned sample size was reached because continued enrollment was no longer feasible. Among 113 screened patients, 36 of a planned 62 were randomized, and 35 were analyzed (18 standard care, 17 intervention). The intervention group received a lower protocol bolus volume during the 6-hour intervention window than the standard-care group (250 [125-500] vs. 650 [500-1500] mL; between-group difference, - 500 mL [95% CI, - 750 to - 250]). Cumulative fluid exposure from pre-randomization through the end of the protocol window was similar between groups (3375 [2375-3875] vs. 3750 [1875-4851] mL; between-group difference, - 150 mL [95% CI, - 1470 to 1250]). The primary outcome favored the intervention: median ΔPaO2:FiO2 was 40.5 [24.0-58.5] versus - 37.9 [-69.2 to -12.5]; p < 0.001 (between-group median difference + 78.3 points; 95% CI 50.5 to 110.0), and 0-6-hour changes in lactate and capillary refill time did not differ.

Conclusion: Because the trial was stopped early, the effect of a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy on oxygenation remains uncertain. A larger trial would be needed to determine whether this strategy improves oxygenation. Such a trial appears feasible.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT06568744, registered August 21, 2024.
